page_title: Why Physics: One Blueprint, Printed Twice

isomorphisms.name: Second Law / BC2 Isomorphism
isomorphisms.chi_law: dS/dt >= 0 (physical) maps to dS_moral/dt >= 0 (theological) under bijection preserving inequality direction and system closure conditions
isomorphisms.physics_process: Second Law of Thermodynamics: entropy of an isolated system never decreases; local decreases require external energy input; heat death is final equilibrium
isomorphisms.theological_phenomenon: Moral entropy: moral disorder increases in a system without Grace; Grace acts as external energy input; sanctification is local order at global cost; complete refusal leads to moral heat death
isomorphisms.prediction: If the isomorphism holds, then any intervention of Grace should produce a measurable local decrease in moral entropy (sanctification) with a corresponding global increase (cost borne by Grace), analogous to a refrigerator.
physics_process_steps: External energy input: allows local dS/dt < 0
Heat death: maximum entropy, no free energy
mapped_text_steps: Grace (G) input: allows local moral order (sanctification)
Global moral entropy still increases (cost borne by G)
Complete moral entropy: refusal completed, no capacity for good
preserved_transitions: Isolated system -> external energy input: maps to system without Grace -> Grace input
Local entropy decrease -> global entropy increase: maps to sanctification -> global cost borne by G
Heat death -> final state: maps to complete moral entropy -> final state
isomorphisms.notes: Mapping is explicit and bijective. The Monte Carlo test claims 8 sigma significance. However, the theological domain lacks quantitative measurement of moral entropy, so empirical verification is currently impossible. The structural correspondence is strong but the prediction is not yet testable.

isomorphisms.name: Conservation Laws / Faithfulness Isomorphism
isomorphisms.chi_law: Conservation of quantity Q (dQ/dt = 0) maps to faithfulness: what is given is not withdrawn
isomorphisms.physics_process: Noether's theorem: every continuous symmetry yields a conserved quantity (e.g., energy, momentum, charge). Conserved quantities remain constant over time in closed systems.
isomorphisms.theological_phenomenon: Divine faithfulness: God's gifts, promises, and character are not withdrawn; they remain constant over time and are not subject to change.
physics_process_steps: Conserved quantity is invariant over time
mapped_text_steps: Faithfulness as a property of God's character
Gifts and promises are not revoked
preserved_transitions: Symmetry -> conservation: maps to divine nature -> faithfulness
missing_transitions: No explicit mapping for the mathematical derivation (Noether's theorem) in the theological domain
isomorphisms.notes: The mapping is suggestive but lacks the formal derivation present in the Second Law example. The theological side does not have an equivalent of Noether's theorem. The correspondence is more analogical than isomorphic at the level of derivation.

isomorphisms.name: Symmetry / Impartiality Isomorphism
isomorphisms.chi_law: Physical laws are invariant under certain transformations (e.g., translation, rotation) -> God's law does not play favorites
isomorphisms.physics_process: Physical laws are the same everywhere and everywhen (spacetime translation invariance) and in all orientations (rotational invariance). No privileged reference frame.
isomorphisms.theological_phenomenon: Divine impartiality: God shows no favoritism; moral law applies equally to all persons regardless of status, time, or place.
physics_process_steps: Laws invariant under translation in space and time
mapped_text_steps: Moral law applies equally to all people
No person is exempt from moral accountability
preserved_transitions: Invariance under transformation -> no privileged frame: maps to universal applicability -> no exemption
missing_transitions: Theological domain lacks a formal symmetry group or transformation rules
isomorphisms.notes: The mapping is conceptually clear but lacks formal mathematical structure on the theological side. It is a strong analogy but not a full isomorphism.

isomorphisms.name: Boundary Conditions / Covenant Isomorphism
isomorphisms.chi_law: Boundary conditions constrain the solution space of differential equations -> covenant constrains the relationship between God and humanity
isomorphisms.physics_process: Boundary conditions specify the values of a solution at the boundaries of a domain; they determine which particular solution is selected from a family of general solutions.
isomorphisms.theological_phenomenon: Covenant: God's chosen constraints on the relationship with humanity; they define the terms of the relationship and determine the outcome (blessing or curse) based on adherence.
physics_process_steps: Differential equation has a family of solutions
Boundary conditions select a unique solution
Solution is determined by the constraints
mapped_text_steps: God's will has many possible outcomes
Covenant terms select a specific relationship path
Outcome is determined by adherence to covenant
preserved_transitions: Family of solutions -> boundary conditions: maps to many possibilities -> covenant terms
missing_transitions: No explicit mapping for the mathematical uniqueness theorem in theology
isomorphisms.notes: The mapping is plausible but the theological side lacks the formal constraint specification. The idea that covenant 'selects' a unique outcome is not as rigorous as boundary conditions in PDEs.

isomorphisms.name: Entropy / Cost of Freedom Isomorphism
isomorphisms.domain_a: Physics (Entropy increase as cost of local order)
isomorphisms.domain_b: Theology (Moral disorder as cost of free will)
isomorphisms.chi_law: Local decrease in entropy requires global increase (dS_total >= 0) -> local moral order (sanctification) requires global cost (Grace bears the disorder)
isomorphisms.physics_process: To create local order (e.g., a refrigerator), you must dump heat elsewhere, increasing total entropy. The Second Law is not violated; the cost is paid globally.
isomorphisms.theological_phenomenon: Free will allows moral disorder; to restore local moral order (sanctification) without violating free will, Grace must absorb the cost of the disorder globally (the Cross).
isomorphisms.prediction: The cost of sanctification (local moral order) must be borne by an external agent (Grace) and must result in a net increase in moral entropy elsewhere (the Cross as global entropy dump).
mapped_text_steps: Sin and disorder transferred to Christ (Cross)
Net moral entropy increases (cost of sin is real)
preserved_transitions: Local order -> global entropy increase: maps to sanctification -> global cost
Heat dump -> environment: maps to sin transfer -> Cross
isomorphisms.notes: This is a strong mapping that parallels the Second Law/BC2 mapping. The cost-bearing mechanism is explicit in both domains. However, the theological side lacks a quantitative measure of 'moral entropy' to verify the prediction.
